name: Uttapam
cuisine: South Indian (Tamil Nadu / Karnataka; an Udupi-restaurant staple across Mumbai)

ingredients.name: Idli / dosa batter, fermented (homemade from the rice, urad dal and methi below, or store-bought)
– Idli rice or dosa rice (parboiled or raw short-grain), for homemade batter
– Split skinless urad dal (white urad / ulundu), for homemade batter
– Fenugreek seeds (methi dana), for homemade batter
– Salt, in the batter
ingredients.householdMeasure: a scant ¼ tsp (batch: about ⅔ tsp)

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.householdMeasure: ½ small onion, finely chopped (about ⅓ cup)

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.householdMeasure: ½ small tomato, finely chopped (about ¼ cup)

ingredients.name: Oil (groundnut or sunflower)
ingredients.householdMeasure: 2 tsp in total: ¼ tsp to grease the tawa + ¾ tsp to drizzle, per uttapam

equipment: Flat tawa or griddle, cast iron or non-stick, at least 20 cm
Lid that covers the tawa (or a large steel plate turned upside down)
Flat spatula (turner) for pressing the topping and flipping
Ladle or a ⅓-cup measure for the batter
Knife, chopping board, small bowl for the topping
For homemade batter only: two bowls for soaking, a mixer-grinder with a wet-grinding jar (or a stone wet grinder), and a large container with room for the batter to double
Measuring cups and spoons (a normal teacup and teaspoons are fine stand-ins)

steps.title: Wash the rice
steps.text: Put 1 cup (200 g) idli or dosa rice in a bowl, cover with water, rub gently and drain. Repeat 2 more times.
steps.visualCue: The last rinse water is only slightly cloudy.
steps.cameraCheck: The bowl of washed rice
steps.videoShot: Hands swirling rice in cloudy water.

steps.title: Wash the urad dal and methi
steps.text: In a second bowl, wash ⅓ cup (65 g) urad dal with ¼ tsp (1.5 g) fenugreek seeds the same way, 3 times.
steps.visualCue: White dal, with a few yellow methi seeds, in clear-ish water.
steps.cameraCheck: The bowl of dal and methi
steps.videoShot: Water draining from the white dal.

steps.title: Soak both
steps.text: Cover each bowl with about 2 cm of fresh water and leave both to soak.
steps.visualCue: The grains look plumper and paler; a rice grain breaks easily between your nails.
steps.cameraCheck: The two soaking bowls
steps.videoShot: Water poured over each bowl.

steps.title: Grind the urad dal
steps.text: Drain the dal and methi (keep the soaking water) and grind with about ⅓ cup cold water, added little by little, until smooth and fluffy.
steps.tip: Cold water keeps the batter cool, which helps it rise.
steps.visualCue: Very smooth, light and airy, like whipped cream; a drop floats in water.
steps.cameraCheck: A spoon of the ground dal batter
steps.videoShot: Fluffy white batter lifted on a spoon.

steps.title: Grind the rice
steps.text: Drain the rice and grind it with about ½ cup water until it is smooth but very slightly grainy, like fine rava.
steps.visualCue: Rubbed between your fingers it feels faintly gritty.
steps.cameraCheck: The rice batter in the jar
steps.videoShot: Rice batter poured from the jar into a big container.

steps.title: Mix and salt
steps.text: Put both batters in a large container, add about ⅔ tsp (3.5 g) salt, and mix with your clean hand for 1 minute.
steps.tip: Hand mixing adds natural microbes and warmth that help fermentation.
steps.visualCue: One even, thick, pourable batter, filling no more than half the container.
steps.cameraCheck: The mixed batter in the container
steps.videoShot: A hand folding the two batters together.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Cover loosely and leave in a warm place (inside a switched-off oven with the light on, in cooler months).
steps.visualCue: The batter has risen to about double, has bubbles on top and smells pleasantly sour.
steps.cameraCheck: The risen batter in the container
steps.videoShot: The lid lifted to show the bubbly, risen batter.

steps.title: Stir down and portion
steps.text: Stir the batter gently, then take out 180 g (about ¾ cup) for this serving. Refrigerate the rest (4–5 days).
steps.visualCue: ¾ cup thick batter in a bowl.
steps.cameraCheck: The ¾ cup batter in the bowl
steps.videoShot: Batter ladled into a small bowl.

steps.title: Check the consistency
steps.text: Lift a ladle of batter and let it fall. If it drops in lumps, stir in 1 tsp water at a time (up to 1 tbsp).
steps.tip: Too thin and the uttapam stays flat; too thick and the centre stays raw.
steps.visualCue: Thick but pourable: it flows in a thick ribbon, thicker than dosa batter, thinner than idli batter.
steps.cameraCheck: Batter falling from the ladle
steps.videoShot: A thick ribbon of batter falling back into the bowl.

steps.title: Measure the batter (ready-batter start)
steps.text: If using store-bought or fridge batter, bring 180 g (about ¾ cup) to room temperature for 15 min while you chop, and check it as in step 9.
steps.visualCue: Batter no longer fridge-cold and pours in a thick ribbon.
steps.cameraCheck: The ¾ cup batter in the bowl
steps.videoShot: Batter poured from a pouch into a bowl.

steps.title: Chop the onion
steps.text: Peel and finely chop 40 g onion (half a small onion).
steps.visualCue: Small, even pieces, about ⅓ cup.
steps.cameraCheck: The chopped onion on the board
steps.videoShot: A knife dicing onion.

steps.title: Chop the tomato
steps.text: Finely chop 40 g tomato (half a small tomato). Scoop out the watery seeds if the tomato is very juicy.
steps.visualCue: Small red cubes, about ¼ cup, not swimming in juice.
steps.cameraCheck: The chopped tomato
steps.videoShot: Tomato cubes pushed into a pile.

steps.title: Chop the chilli and coriander
steps.text: Finely chop 1 small green chilli (3 g) and 1 tbsp coriander leaves (4 g).
steps.visualCue: Tiny green flecks.
steps.cameraCheck: The chilli and coriander on the board
steps.videoShot: A knife running through coriander.

steps.title: Mix the topping
steps.text: Put onion, tomato, chilli and coriander in a bowl, add a small pinch (0.3 g) salt, and mix. Split it into 2 equal heaps.
steps.tip: Salt the topping only now; salted tomato and onion release water if they sit.
steps.visualCue: A colourful mix in two equal heaps.
steps.cameraCheck: The two topping heaps
steps.videoShot: The topping tossed with a spoon.

steps.title: Heat and grease the tawa
steps.text: Heat the tawa on medium for 2 min, then spread ¼ tsp oil over it with a folded paper towel or half an onion.
steps.visualCue: A few drops of water sprinkled on it sizzle and vanish in 2–3 seconds.
steps.cameraCheck: The greased, hot tawa
steps.videoShot: Water drops sizzling on the tawa.

steps.title: Pour the first uttapam
steps.text: Pour half the batter (90 g, about ⅓ cup + 1 tbsp) in the centre and spread it gently with the back of the ladle into a 13 cm circle, about 1 cm thick.
steps.tip: Do not spread it thin like a dosa; 2–3 light circles are enough.
steps.visualCue: A thick, round, even pancake; small bubbles start to appear.
steps.cameraCheck: The batter circle on the tawa
steps.videoShot: The ladle making two slow circles.

steps.title: Add the topping
steps.text: Immediately scatter one heap of topping over the batter and press it in lightly with the spatula.
steps.visualCue: The vegetables are half sunk in the wet batter.
steps.cameraCheck: The topped uttapam
steps.videoShot: The spatula pressing onion and tomato into the batter.

steps.title: Drizzle the oil
steps.text: Drizzle ¾ tsp oil around the edge and a few drops over the top.
steps.visualCue: The oil sizzles around the edge.
steps.cameraCheck: Oil around the edge of the uttapam
steps.videoShot: A spoon tracing oil around the edge.

steps.title: Cover and cook
steps.text: Lower the heat to medium-low, cover with a lid and cook.
steps.tip: If the base browns before the top sets, the heat is too high.
steps.visualCue: The top is set, matt and full of holes, with no wet batter; the edge lifts easily and the base is golden.
steps.cameraCheck: The underside lifted on the spatula
steps.videoShot: The lid lifted to show a set, holey top.

steps.title: Flip
steps.text: Flip the uttapam and press it lightly with the spatula.
steps.visualCue: The onion and tomato catch light brown spots and smell sweet; no raw-onion smell.
steps.cameraCheck: The topping side on the tawa
steps.videoShot: The uttapam flipping over.

steps.title: Take it off
steps.text: Flip it back (topping side up) and slide it onto a plate.
steps.visualCue: Golden base, soft thick centre, browned vegetables on top.
steps.cameraCheck: The uttapam on the plate
steps.videoShot: The uttapam sliding onto a steel plate.

steps.title: Make the second uttapam
steps.text: Wipe the tawa, sprinkle a little water to cool it slightly, then repeat steps 15–21 with the rest of the batter, topping and oil.
steps.tip: A tawa that is too hot after the first uttapam makes the second spread unevenly; the water sprinkle fixes it.
steps.visualCue: A second uttapam matching the first.
steps.cameraCheck: Both uttapams on the plate
steps.videoShot: Two uttapams side by side.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot with sambar and coconut chutney.
steps.visualCue: Two thick golden uttapams with colourful topping, steaming.
steps.cameraCheck: The plate with sides
steps.videoShot: A piece torn off and dipped in sambar.

reasons: a fermented rice-and-urad pancake cooked on a tawa with 2 tsp oil, not fried; it is plant-based, has no cholesterol or added sugar, moderate salt (about 1.3 g), about 10 g protein and 5 g fibre, and fermentation makes it easy to digest. Against it: it is mostly white-rice starch (a fairly high glycaemic load) and the protein is modest for a 375 kcal meal. Restaurant versions are often larger, cooked with more oil or butter, saltier, and come with coconut chutney that adds fat.

researchRating.basis: a staple of South Indian breakfast menus and Mumbai Udupi restaurants, with dozens of well-known recipes (Veg Recipes of India, Hebbar's Kitchen, Tarla Dalal, My Food Story, Fun Food Frolic, Chitra's Food Book) and a place on almost every South Indian delivery menu (marked "Bestseller" on some Swiggy listings; magicpin reviews of Manohar Pure Veg, Matunga, single out its tomato-onion uttapam). It is a little less celebrated than masala dosa or idli, and a thick uttapam can turn out doughy or raw in the centre for beginners. Recipe-review vote counts could not be checked in this run.

storage: Cooked uttapam is best eaten fresh; it turns chewy as it cools. Fridge: up to 1 day in an airtight box, within 2 hours of cooking. Freezer: not recommended (the topping turns soggy). Reheat on a hot tawa for 1 min per side with a few drops of oil, covered; avoid the microwave, which makes it rubbery. Uncooked batter: fridge 4–5 days (it gets more sour, which suits uttapam); freezer up to 1 month, thawed in the fridge overnight.
leftoverRemix: Kothu Uttapam. Tear 2 leftover uttapams into small pieces. In a kadai, heat 1 tsp oil, fry ¼ chopped onion and a few curry leaves, add 2 tbsp leftover sambar (or ¼ tsp sambar masala and a splash of water) and the uttapam pieces, and toss on high heat for 3–4 min, chopping with the spatula like kothu parotta. Finish with coriander and lemon (add a beaten egg for an eggetarian version): soft breakfast turned into a spicy, crumbly street-style snack.
burnOff: about 5.4 km of running (375 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 7.5 km of brisk walking (about 1 h 30 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.). With the usual sambar and chutney (about +150–200 kcal), add about 2–3 km of running.

navratri.reason: the batter is rice and urad dal (a grain and a pulse) and it is topped with onion, all avoided on the common North and West Indian vrat rule set; a samak (barnyard millet) uttapam would be a different batter

ekadashi.reason: rice and dals (urad) are the main foods given up on Ekadashi

jain.reason: skip the onion; rice, urad dal, tomato, chilli and coriander fit common Jain practice (some stricter Jain families avoid overnight-fermented foods; not verified in this run, so check family practice)

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, so there is no halal concern; light, filling and easy to digest, with moderate salt (about 1.3 g)

jain.reason: skip the onion (a root/bulb); top with tomato, capsicum, green chilli and coriander instead

vegan.reason: rice, urad dal, vegetables and oil only; no ghee, butter or curd in the main recipe (restaurant "butter uttapam" versions are not vegan)

pescatarian.reason: vegetarian, no meat, fish or egg, so it fits a pescatarian diet

sattvik.reason: skip the onion and use tomato, coriander and curry leaves (no garlic is used anyway)

glutenFree.reason: rice and urad dal batter with no wheat, rava or hing in the main recipe; check the label on store-bought batter, and note that rava (semolina) uttapam is not gluten-free

dairyFree.reason: no dairy; cooked in oil, not ghee or butter

description: A vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free and dairy-free South Indian pancake of fermented rice-and-urad batter topped with onion and tomato; Jain, sattvik and instant versions below.

variants.reason: . Main recipe already vegan (oil, no ghee or butter). Restaurant "butter" uttapams are not.
. Main recipe already gluten-free (rice and urad dal, no hing). Use a store-bought batter whose label shows no wheat, and avoid rava uttapam.
